title: The Mystery of the Missing Medal
markdown:
The Sparkle and Shine festival was just around the corner. Bunting strung itself across every lamppost as if it had somewhere important to be. The air buzzed like a million tiny bumblebees doing a disco dance. Mrs. Higgins’s triple-chocolate fudge cake smelled so rich it made teeth ache just from walking past. And the gleaming glittery absolutely fabulous prize medal for the festival competition had gone missing. Poof. Vanished like a sock in the laundry.

It was last seen on a velvet cushion, perched proudly inside the very top of the old Bell Tower. And who was perched even higher, keeping a watchful beady eye on everything? Pia the parrot. Her feathers shimmered like a spilled paint pot: emerald green, sapphire blue, ruby red, and sunshine yellow swirled together. A rainbow on wings. She could mimic anything. A squeaky door hinge. The rumble of Mr. Grumbles’s belly after his third plate of stew. The mournful hoot of an owl on a moonlit night. Nailed it.

Pia was doing her usual sunbathing and squawking practice near the Bell Tower window, letting out a particularly enthusiastic series of clicks and whistles, when she heard it. Not the usual dong-dong-DONG of the bell. A faint sneaky little clink-scrape. Clink-scrape. It sounded like a mischievous whisper trying to hide behind a shout.

She tilted her head, beady eyes narrowed, colourful plumage ruffling. "What is that little scratchy noise?" She mimicked it herself, voice surprisingly high and tinny. "Clink-scrape. A tiny metal mouse wearing boots and carrying a tiny toolbox." She giggled, a sound like tiny bells shaking.

She fluttered down to the next ledge, a perfect spot for a better view. And there she saw Brik. Brik was a gargoyle, not the spooky sort that makes you hide under the covers. He was made of lovely smooth grey stone, cool and comforting to the touch. Eyes as round and kind as two polished marbles. He was usually quite quiet, just sitting there being a gargoyle, stony chin on stony hands, looking for all the world as if he were contemplating the meaning of life. Most people thought gargoyles sat and looked grumpy, scaring away pigeons. Brik observed. Always.

"Brik. Brik." Pia landed on his shoulder with a gentle rustle that tickled his stony ear. "Did you hear that? That clink-scrape. Terribly peculiar."

Brik blinked his large marble eyes. He rarely spoke, mostly because he did not have much to say that could not be conveyed with a nod or a thoughtful tilt of his head. When he did speak, it was a low rumble, like pebbles settling at the bottom of a quiet stream. "I heard something." He pointed a sturdy stone finger, thick as a tree branch, toward a high inaccessible ledge. "Up there. Too small for me to reach easily. The wind is quite strong up there too."

Pia puffed out her chest, rainbow feathers catching the sunlight. "Too small for you, maybe. Not for Pia. Detective duty. The game is a-wing. Clink-scrape." She zipped off, a streak of joy and determination against the bright blue sky.

The ledge was high. The village spread out beneath her like a toy town. Ancient stone groaned softly in the wind. A playful chilly breeze tickled her neck feathers. She peered into a shadowy crevice between two moss-covered stones. The air tasted of damp earth and old secrets, and a faint metallic tang prickled her beak. Wedged tight was a single tiny glinting bit of metal. Not the medal itself. A tiny piece that had broken off.

"Fiddlesticks. Someone has been a bit clumsy with the prize. A sparkly disaster."

She flew back down to Brik, who was still watching with those wide thoughtful marble eyes, stony brow furrowed. "It is gone. The medal. Really gone. But I found a little shiny bit. A clue." She dropped the tiny metal shard at his stony feet. It looked like a sliver of a forgotten star, once part of something much grander.

Brik picked it up carefully with his stone fingers, touch surprisingly delicate for something so heavy. He turned it over and over. "This looks like the little star from the edge of the medal." He looked toward the bottom of the tower, where a thin almost invisible trail of dust seemed to lead away from the base. "And there is a trail. Of dust. From the crevice. Small dust."

"Dust?" Pia hopped, tail feathers fanning. "Tiny dusty footprints. A proper mystery. Follow the dust. Follow the clues." She fluttered ahead, then zipped back, impatient. "Come on, slow-pokes. My feathers are tingling."

Brik followed with silent strength and a steady pace. The dust trail led them past the baker’s shop, where the air was thick and warm with cinnamon and warm bread. A blur of movement near a pile of flour sacks. A tiny quick shadow that flitted and darted.

"Was that it?" Pia tilted her head, sharp eyes trying to catch the fleeting shape. "It looked small. And fast. Like a runaway biscuit that had escaped the baker’s oven."

"Too quick," Brik rumbled, missing nothing. "And no clink-scrape. Just a rustle."

They followed the dusty path further, past giggling children playing hopscotch, shouts echoing merrily. The sun dipped lower, painting the clouds orange, pink, and fiery red. The festival drums would start any minute. The tower clock, which had always been a polite neighbour, suddenly felt like a heartbeat urging them on.

Suddenly Pia shrieked. "I hear it again. Clink-scrape. Louder. From the old clock maker’s workshop." The door was slightly ajar, as if someone had just hurried out, and a tiny sliver of warm light peeked from the gap.

Brik nudged the door open with his shoulder. It creaked like an old man stretching. Inside, surrounded by the constant rhythmic ticking of a hundred clocks, the whirring of tiny gears, and the delicate springs of countless timepieces, sat Meilyr Button. Meilyr was a mischievous little dormouse, known throughout the village for his love of shiny things and his incredibly fast nimble little paws. He was trying, with all his might, to polish the Sparkle and Shine medal with a bit of velvet cloth. The tiny star-shaped piece Brik held now fitted perfectly back onto its edge. He had been trying to smooth out a tiny scratch he had accidentally made, causing that peculiar clink-scrape.

Meilyr squeaked in surprise and dropped the medal with a soft thump onto the wooden floor. "Oh. Oops. Hello." His little nose twitched.

Pia landed on a tall grandfather clock, bright feathers a stark contrast to the dusty workshop. "Meilyr. You little rascal. You took the medal. You know you are not supposed to touch things that are not yours."

Brik stepped forward, large stone form filling the doorway. He held out the tiny star piece, its glint catching the light. "You broke it a little. And then you tried to hide it. And fix it."

Meilyr wrung his tiny paws, whiskers drooping like wilted flowers. "I am so sorry. It was just so shiny. I might have dropped it when I was admiring it. I just wanted to make it perfect again for the festival. I did not want anyone to be sad. I only wanted to help make it sparkle." He looked genuinely remorseful, small body trembling.

Pia tilted her head, beady eyes softening. "You certainly made us a bit worried, little squeaker. And the Mayor too. But you were trying to fix it. Good intentions. Very, very bad execution."

Brik nodded, marble eyes kind. "We can forgive you for trying. Next time, ask. Or leave it for the humans to handle. Or perhaps ask Pia for advice on polishing."

Just then the first booming notes of the festival drums echoed through the air, a magnificent resonant sound that vibrated through the very stones of the workshop. "The festival," squeaked Meilyr, eyes wide. "And I still have the medal. And it is not perfectly fixed."

"Not for long." Pia scooped up the medal. It was surprisingly light for such a grand prize, a feather in her beak. "Come on, Brik. We have to get this to the podium before the Mayor faints from worry."

With Pia flying ahead, the precious medal clutched carefully, and Brik trotting his surprisingly swift stony trot behind, they dashed out of the workshop. They raced through the now-crowded village square, the air alive with music, laughter, and excited chatter. They arrived just as the Mayor, a jolly man with a magnificent walrus moustache that twitched with anxiety, was about to announce that the medal was lost forever. His face was as pale as unused icing.

"Ta-da." Pia flew in a magnificent arc over the Mayor’s head, a blur of rainbow colours, and landed with a dramatic flourish on the prize podium. The medal gleamed in the warm torchlight.

The crowd gasped, then erupted into cheers. Pia dropped the medal onto its velvet cushion, right where it belonged. Brik stood tall beside her, a picture of quiet strength. A faint happy rumble, like a tiny earthquake, vibrated in his chest. Meilyr, looking sheepish but proud, scurried up and nudged the medal with his nose, a silent apology.

The Mayor, moustache now twitching with relief, beamed at them. "Pia. Brik. You saved the Sparkle and Shine. And you too, Meilyr, for helping to fix it." He chuckled, eyes twinkling. "It seems our quiet gargoyle and our chatty parrot are quite the detective team. A most unusual, but most effective, partnership."

Pia preened, puffing out her chest. "We heard the clues. We followed the trail. We solved the mystery. A piece of cake. Or a piece of shiny medal that needed a bit of polishing."

Brik gave a rare small smile, a subtle softening of his stony features. He nudged Pia gently with his stony head. She chirped happily. For the rest of the festival the rainbow parrot and the shy gargoyle were the undisputed heroes of the day. The medal sparkled brighter than ever, and Meilyr Button, who had only wanted to make it shine, stayed close enough to be useful and far enough not to polish anything else without asking.
characters: Pia (rainbow parrot), Brik (shy gargoyle), Meilyr (mischievous dormouse)
